en: Mayon Volcano in Albay exhibits a nearly perfect symmetrical cone shape formed by layers of cooled lava and volcanic ash.
The Pasig River in Metro Manila is a tidal river that reverses its observable flow direction depending on the ocean tides.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River in Palawan contains a massive cave system where visitors can observe stalactites and stalagmites forming from dripping water.
The grass-covered mounds of the Chocolate Hills in Bohol turn brown during the dry season due to a lack of rainfall.
The coral atolls of Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park in the Sulu Sea are formed by the accumulated calcium carbonate skeletons of tiny marine polyps.
Observers in Donsol, Sorsogon can spot whale sharks, the largest living fish species, filtering plankton near the water surface.
The Banaue Rice Terraces in Ifugao demonstrate an ancient, observable irrigation system that channels mountain rainwater down stepped agricultural slopes.
Taal Volcano in Batangas exhibits a unique geological structure with a crater lake situated on an island inside a larger lake.
The towering limestone cliffs of El Nido in Palawan were formed over millions of years by the accumulation of marine corals and shells.
The mangrove trees along the Loboc River in Bohol host colonies of fireflies that produce light through a chemical reaction called bioluminescence.
The observable Amihan season in the Philippines occurs when cool northeast monsoon winds bring dry weather and lower temperatures from November to February.
Observers at the peak of Mount Pulag in Benguet can see a dwarf cloud forest where persistent fog and cold temperatures stunt plant growth.
